questiontext.text:
The plan shows a plot of land beside a stream near Nyeri. A straight road runs along the bottom, there is a fence at each end, and the stream forms the curved edge. Each square stands for \({@dx@}\,\text{m}\) along the road and \({@dy@}\,\text{m}\) away from it.

A full square lies wholly inside the plot. A part square has the curve passing through it.

(a) How many full squares are there?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

(b) How many part squares are there?

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(c) What area does one square stand for?

[[input:ans3]] \(\text{m}^2\) [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt2]]

(d) Estimate the area of the plot.

[[input:ans4]] \(\text{m}^2\) [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt3]]

There are \(F = {@nF@}\) full squares and \(P = {@nP@}\) part squares. A part square is, on average, about half covered, so the estimate is \({@nF@} + \tfrac{1}{2} \times {@nP@} = {@est@}\) squares.

One square is a rectangle \({@dx@}\,\text{m}\) by \({@dy@}\,\text{m}\) on the ground, so it stands for \({@dx@} \times {@dy@} = {@sqa@}\,\text{m}^2\).

Area \(\approx {@est@} \times {@sqa@} = {@area@}\,\text{m}^2\).

Hand counts can differ by a square, so counts within \(1\) of these were accepted.

questiondescription.text:
Area Approximations: counting squares under a curve

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.2 (a) / Essential 2.1 (a): Count the full and part squares under a curve on a grid whose squares stand for different lengths across and up, and estimate the area in square metres.

Core and Essential

This question is original to this project.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core and Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: Some of the squares you counted as full have the curve passing through them. Count those as part squares.
You have missed some part squares. Count every square the curve passes through, even if only a little of the plot is inside it.

falsefeedback.text: Count again: first the squares wholly inside the plot, then every square the curve passes through.

feedbackvariables.text: oneside: is(ans3 = dx or ans3 = dy);

truefeedback.text: You added the two sides. The area of a rectangle is width \(\times\) height: \({@dx@} \times {@dy@}\).
That is the perimeter of one square, not its area.
That is the length of one side only. Multiply the width by the height.

falsefeedback.text: One square on the plan is a rectangle \({@dx@}\,\text{m}\) by \({@dy@}\,\text{m}\) on the ground. Its area is not \({@ans3@}\,\text{m}^2\).

feedbackvariables.text: okc: is(abs(ans1-nF) <= 1 and abs(ans2-nP) <= 1 and ans3 = sqa); dok: is(abs(ans1-nF) <= 1 and abs(ans2-nP) <= 1 and abs(ans4-sqa*(ans1+ans2/2)) < 1/1000);

falsefeedback.text: Your method is right for your answers to (a) to (c), but check them.

truefeedback.text: You counted each part square as a whole square. Each part square counts as half.
You left out the part squares. Add half of them to the full squares before multiplying.
That is the estimate in squares. Multiply by the area of one square.

falsefeedback.text: Area \(=\) (number of squares) \(\times\) (area of one square). Your answers give \({@ans1@} + \tfrac{1}{2} \times {@ans2@}\) squares of \({@ans3@}\,\text{m}^2\) each, and that does not come to \({@ans4@}\,\text{m}^2\).

truefeedback.text: Your area is right for your counts in (a) and (b). Your answer to (c) is not the area that one square stands for, so check (c).
